children: SYDNEY--Minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia's November meeting reveal division on the board over the pace of interest-rate increases, but continued agreement on the need to be ready to tighten further if necessary.

"Members noted that inflation was still too high and forecast to remain so for another year," the minutes showed. "Members...still viewed the risks to the latest inflation forecast as being skewed to the upside."
The decision to raise rates in November marked the RBA's fifth hike of the year, making it one of the central banks that has been most aggressive in fighting inflation.
The RBA's Monetary Policy Board was split six to three in favor of delivering the latest increase in the official cash rate to 4.85%.
Economists now expect the Australian central bank to remain on hold for a while in order to assess inflation data as it comes in.
Earlier on Tuesday, RBA Governor Michele Bullock said inflation risks remain biased to the upside, adding that the inflation problem Australians face isn't merely the result of higher oil prices.
A boom in data-center construction to build out capacity for artificial intelligence is also adding to demand, she added.
The RBA board still senses that the economy is operating with excess demand, and inflation isn't expected to return to its target of 2.5% until mid-2028.
Economic growth is forecast to be stronger in the near term than had been expected in August, driven by a stronger outlook for investment.

"The case to raise the cash rate target by 25 basis points at this meeting was founded on concerns about the further deterioration in the outlook for inflation, continued upside risks to the inflation forecast and an assessment that financial conditions may not be as restrictive as that backdrop required," the November minutes showed.

title: RBA Board Split But Still Focused on Upward Inflation Risks
